turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Um... I guess what brings me in is that I keep getting hit, just completely out of nowhere, with this memory. It's the scene of my cousin on that pavement. 

It's so real, like... I can actually hear the shouting and see the lights all over again. And it happens even when I'm just standing in the church office, trying to do my work and act normal. It just takes over.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient describes experiencing sudden, involuntary, and vivid intrusive memories of a traumatic event involving their cousin, which feel very real and disrupt their daily life.

turns.doctor_question: How long ago did this traumatic event occur?
turns.patient_response: Um, it was two years and three months ago. That's when my cousin was killed. And... yeah, this has just been going on ever since then.

turns.doctor_question: When these memories take over, do you ever feel like you are somehow detached from your body or that the world around you feels unreal or dreamlike?
turns.patient_response: Um, no, I don't think I've ever felt like that. I don't feel detached from my body or anything. And the world around me doesn't really feel like a dream... it's just that the memory itself is so intense and loud that it kind of demands all my attention. But I still know I'm me, in my own body, when it happens.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient describes their memories as being 'so intense and loud that it kind of demands all my attention', indicating intrusive symptoms.
symptom_reasoning.S082: The patient explicitly denies feeling detached from their body or feeling like the world around them is unreal or dreamlike.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself going out of your way to avoid certain places, people, or activities that remind you of what happened to your cousin?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, I definitely do. Um... I actually take the long way around town now, just so I don't have to pass the community center or that court. And if somebody brings it up—like, if people start talking about that night—I just shut it down. Or I'll find some reason to excuse myself and leave the room. I just don't want to be around anything that brings it up.

symptom_reasoning.S070: The patient explicitly confirms avoiding places like the community center and court, as well as conversations that remind them of the traumatic event.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any changes in your sleep patterns, such as difficulty falling or staying asleep, since this happened?
turns.patient_response: Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think I've had any major issues with my sleep. I usually fall asleep okay, and I stay asleep through the night. It's just the daytime stuff that's really hard to deal with.

symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient explicitly states they have not had major issues with sleep, falling asleep okay and staying asleep through the night.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed yourself feeling more irritable or having sudden outbursts of anger since this happened?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, I have. It's... it's actually been a real problem at work. I'm in ministry, and lately I've just snapped in meetings over really small things. I've caught myself raising my voice at the deacons or the youth leaders, almost treating them like they're the enemy. It just flares up out of nowhere, and afterward, I just really hate how fast I went there. It's not like me at all.

symptom_reasoning.S060: The patient describes reacting sharply to minor stimuli by snapping in meetings over really small things.
symptom_reasoning.S077: The patient confirms having sudden angry outbursts with little provocation, specifically mentioning raising their voice at colleagues.

turns.doctor_question: Since this happened, do you find yourself feeling constantly on guard, or do you find that you are easily startled by sudden noises or movements?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, I do. Um, I'm constantly on guard now. Like, I can't even sit with my back to a door anymore. And when I'm at church events, I'm just... I'm always watching people's hands, checking the corners, watching cars if they slow down outside. I spend more time looking for the nearest exit than I do actually paying attention to the people right in front of me. I'm just always waiting for something to happen.

symptom_reasoning.S079: The patient explicitly states they are constantly on guard, cannot sit with their back to a door, and are always scanning their environment for threats and exits.
